acceptedAnswer.text: Custom crating means a crate built around one item — measured to that piece, not pulled from a stack of stock boxes. Inside, the piece is blocked, braced and cushioned so it cannot move in transit. Packing wraps an item in flexible protection; a crate gives it a rigid shell that freight systems can stack and handle.

mainEntity.name: When does a piece need a custom crate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Five triggers settle it, and any one is enough: the structure itself is fragile — thin glass, stone tops, delicate carvings, fine finishes; the journey has hand-offs between vehicles or terminals; the shape defeats padding, because oversized or irregular pieces cannot be anchored with straps and pads alone; the piece is crossing a border; or the piece is going into storage, where stacking pressure and contact from other freight last for months.

Padding handles abrasion and minor impact, and nothing more — it cannot carry a load stacked on it, stop a puncture, or fix a piece against a shifting load. When a piece is sturdily built, its exposure is surface-level scratches and scuffs, one crew carries it once in one truck, and the destination is a room rather than a warehouse shelf, blankets and stretch wrap are the complete answer. A standard mirror can travel in a mirror carton; the line is whether a failure would be a scuff or a fracture.

mainEntity.name: Does an export crate play by different rules?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — the wood becomes part of the regulation. ISPM 15, the International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures No. 15, governs solid wood packaging in international trade: the solid wood must be treated and marked, and wood packaging that does not comply can be delayed, treated at the shipper's cost, or refused. Manufactured wood such as plywood and oriented strand board is exempt; a crate's solid-wood frame and skids are not. Our export packing and crating work is built to the ISPM 15 standard from compliant, heat-treated, marked wood. The company claims no ISPM 15 certification.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a crate, a pallet and a skid?

acceptedAnswer.text: A skid is a base — runners that carry a load and let handling gear underneath. A pallet is a flat deck on the same principle. Neither has walls. A crate is the base plus an enclosure: panels and a lid that turn protection from a platform into a structure, with the interior fitted so the piece cannot shift.

mainEntity.name: Can a custom crate be reused?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes — many custom-built crates are reusable, which spreads the build cost across future moves. Whether a crate suits a second journey depends on its construction and the next piece, so reuse is settled when the next job is scoped, not assumed.

We publish no per-crate price list. Crating is scoped per job — the piece is surveyed and measured, and the crate designed around its weight, fragile points and center of mass — and quoted inside the one flat rate in writing before move day, never hourly.

acceptedAnswer.text: Heavy pieces are planned, not improvised. A piece in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band is planned under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol, with the floor check referencing L/360, and its crating is scoped inside the same written flat-rate job.
